parts.overview: Ostra is a local server that runs an engineering pipeline. A user describes a task in a browser console. The code-driven engine classifies the task, runs agents (models with tools) through research, spec, plan, build, review, test, and documentation stages, and stops at gates for user answers. The workspace holds 15 Rust crates, a React console in `web/`, a design system in `design/`, and prompt assets in `assets/`. The `ostra` binary serves the console, a REST API, and a WebSocket. It runs each agent on a native model loop or inside an installed harness CLI. The engine keeps each session as an event log, so a restart continues the work.

sections.title: Architecture and crate map
sections.summary: Names the owner of each concern in the 15 crates, the direction of each dependency, the repository layout, and the build commands.
sections.body:
Ostra is a Rust workspace of 15 crates and a React console. A change lands in the wrong crate when the owner of a behavior is unclear. This page names the owner of each concern and the direction of each dependency.

## What Ostra does

Ostra is a local server that runs an engineering pipeline. A user describes a task in the browser console. The engine splits the task into stages. Each stage runs an agent, which is a model with tools and a fixed role. At a gate, the engine stops and waits for an answer from the user.

The binary is `ostra`. Its entry point is `crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs`. It serves the console, a REST API, and one WebSocket.

## Runtime components

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Browser[Browser console] -->|REST and WebSocket| Server[ostra-server]
    Server --> Workspace[WorkspaceRt]
    Workspace --> Engine[Engine]
    Engine -->|append events| Store[workspace.db]
    Engine -->|Executor trait| Native[Native executor]
    Engine -->|Executor trait| Harness[Harness executor]
    Native --> Providers[Model providers]
    Native --> Tools[Native tools]
    Native --> Policy[Policy engine]
    Tools --> Sandbox[Sandbox]
    Harness -->|PTY| CLI[Harness CLI]
    CLI -->|ostra hook and mcp-stdio| Server
```

The engine does not know how an agent runs. It calls the `Executor` trait from `ostra-core`. The server supplies two implementations: the native executor and the harness executor. The engine reads settings and starts judge calls through the `Services` trait in `crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs`. Because of these traits, the engine tests run with fakes and need no model.

## Crate map

| Crate | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra-core` | Shared types: ids, agents, settings (`config.rs`), session events, wire types for the browser (`api.rs`), paths, pipeline enums, typed documents, books, pricing. |
| `ostra-store` | SQLite storage: `registry.db`, each `workspace.db`, each project lesson store, and encryption of saved credentials. |
| `ostra-agents` | The embedded `assets/` folder, prompt rendering for each executor, typed spawn blocks, and the repo brief. |
| `ostra-engine` | Sessions as event-sourced state, the planner, the runner, judge calls, the init flow, and subagent coordination. |
| `ostra-policy` | Guards and permission rules that check every tool call, and the shell parser behind them. |
| `ostra-sandbox` | The kernel boundary under agent commands: bubblewrap, Seatbelt, the egress proxy, and decoy files. |
| `ostra-tools` | Native tool implementations: file tools, Bash, search, web fetch, memory, documents, and the tool definitions. |
| `ostra-providers` | A neutral chat interface over the Anthropic Messages API and the OpenAI Responses API, plus a scripted provider for tests. |
| `ostra-exec-native` | The native agent loop that runs one execution on an API key. |
| `ostra-exec-harness` | Executors for Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, and Antigravity under a PTY, with the hook bridge and the MCP shim. |
| `ostra-mcp` | A client for external MCP servers over stdio and streamable HTTP, with OAuth. |
| `ostra-code` | Code navigation: tokenizer, per-project index, dependency graph, and language server clients. |
| `ostra-notify` | Web Push message encryption and VAPID signing. |
| `ostra-workspace` | Workspace settings checks, projects, approvals for folder files, workspace creation, and the runtime of an open workspace. |
| `ostra-server` | The `ostra` binary: startup, browser auth, REST and WebSocket API, and the glue that gives each workspace an engine. |

## Dependency direction

The dependency graph has one direction. Lower crates know nothing about higher crates.

- `ostra-core` depends on no other Ostra crate. Every other crate depends on it.
- `ostra-engine` depends on `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, and `ostra-agents`. It does not depend on the executors, the providers, or the policy engine.
- `ostra-exec-native` depends on `ostra-tools`, `ostra-providers`, `ostra-policy`, and `ostra-store`.
- `ostra-exec-harness` depends on `ostra-core` and `ostra-sandbox`.
- `ostra-workspace` depends on the engine, the store, the agents crate, and the policy crate.
- `ostra-server` depends on every other crate and wires them together.

Put a type that the browser, the store, and the engine all use into `ostra-core`. Do not put it into `ostra-engine`, because `ostra-store` depends on `ostra-core` only.

## Repository layout

| Path | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/` | The 15 crates. |
| `assets/` | Agent prompts and `agent.toml` files, judge prompts, stack references, one bundled skill, and `tool-mapping.toml`. `ostra-agents` embeds the folder with `rust-embed`. |
| `web/` | The React console (Vite and TypeScript). The binary embeds `web/dist`. |
| `design/` | The design system package `@ostra/design`. |
| `tests/` | `conformance/main.rs`, `evals/`, `browser/`, and `windows-probes/`. The Cargo workspace excludes `windows-probes`. |
| `.cargo/config.toml` | Sets `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` to `web/src/api/gen`. |
| `build.sh`, `run.sh`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `install.sh`, `install.ps1` | Build, start, and install scripts. |

`.ostra/INVENTORY.md` and the root `package.json` name a `site/` folder. This checkout has no `site/` folder and no `docs/` folder.

## Commands

- Build every crate: `cargo build --workspace`.
- Run every test: `cargo test --workspace`.
- Format every crate: `cargo fmt --all`.
- Build the web console and the release binary: `./build.sh`. The script builds the UI first because the binary embeds `web/dist` at compile time.
- Start Ostra: `./run.sh`. When no port is set, the server tries the 20 ports from 7878 upward.

The toolchain is `1.98.1` (`rust-toolchain.toml`). The workspace uses edition 2024.

## Rule IDs in code comments

Source comments cite rule IDs, for example `Rule D3` or `Rule H2`. The rule text is not in this repository. Read the comment and the code near it. These families appear in the code:

| Prefix | Topic |
| --- | --- |
| `D` | Spec and plan documents, fact-check, format. |
| `T` | Closing gate, tests. |
| `B` | Documentation books. |
| `H` | Waiting runs and subagent coordination. |
| `J` | Judge routing of answers. |
| `C` | Added context: files, amendments, uploads. |
| `P` | Pause, resume, containment, stopped executions. |
| `O` | Project creation and the advisor. |
| `G` | Tool enforcement by guards. |
| `F` | Feedback rounds and the session context file. |
| `A`, `W`, `I` | Approvals, workspace artifacts, init. |

sections.title: Session lifecycle and categories
sections.summary: Explains how a request becomes a session, how the category selects the flow, and how a session pauses, stops, or ends.
sections.body:
A user request must become a fixed order of stages, and the right order depends on the request. A session is one run of the pipeline for one request. The `Classify` judge picks a category, and the category selects the flow. This page lists the flows, the lanes, and the ways a session ends.

## Start of a session

1. The browser creates a session. The engine method is `Engine::create_session`. It refuses a blank request with the message `Describe the task first.`
2. `start_session` appends the `SessionCreated` event. The event holds the request, the options, the projects, attached files, uploads, pinned projects, and the chosen documentation book.
3. The planner sees no category, so it returns a `Step::Judge` for `JudgeKind::Classify`.
4. The judge returns `ClassifyOut`: `category`, `projects`, `explore_tasks`, `opts_in` (tests and docs), `reason`, and a `title` of 2 to 5 words. The engine cuts the title to `TITLE_CHARS` (60 characters).

If the user pinned projects, the pinned set is the whole scope (Rule O6). The classify prompt tells the judge to return exactly those projects.

## Categories and flows

| Category | Request type | Flow after classification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RESEARCH` | Investigate or explain. No change. | Explore tasks, sufficiency check, completion. |
| `SPEC` | Write requirements. | Explore, spec flow without approval, completion. |
| `PLAN` | Design or break down work. | Explore, spec with approval, plan with approval, completion. |
| `IMPLEMENT` | Change code. | Explore, `Track` judge, light or full track, phases, implementation review, closing stages, completion. |
| `VERIFY` | Run the existing tests. Write none. | Phases only, then completion. |
| `TEST` | Write tests for existing code. | Closing stages (execution-path analysis, write-test, review), then completion. |
| `DOCS` | Write a documentation book for existing code. | Docs stage, architecture, book write, then completion. |
| `PROMPT` | Write a prompt, a skill, or an agent file. | Phases with `prompt-generation`. Review runs only when a changed file is not an instruction file. |
| `QUICK_CHANGE` | A small edit that the request fully describes. | One implementer pass on the native executor. |
| `QUICK_ANSWER` | A factual question. | One `quick-answer` execution. Its answer is the completion report. |

The classify prompt tells the judge to pick the category that produces more of the pipeline when two fit. A stage that the request did not need costs one round. A stage that the request needed but lost gives a wrong result.

## Flow of an IMPLEMENT request

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Classify[Classify judge] --> Explore[Explore tasks]
    Explore --> Track{Track judge}
    Track -->|light| Phases[Phases and review loops]
    Track -->|full| Spec[Spec flow with approval]
    Spec --> Stakes{Stakes judge}
    Stakes -->|low| Phases
    Stakes -->|medium or high| Plan[Plan flow with approval]
    Plan --> Phases
    Phases --> Review[Implementation review gate]
    Review --> Closing[Format tests docs book]
    Closing --> Done[Completion judge and report]
```

The light track is the default. The `Track` judge picks `full` only when the research shows one of these: an open requirement, a changed contract, a schema or data change, an ordered change across modules, a security-sensitive change, or a new codebase. A user can force a track with `SessionOptions.track`.

## Lanes and stage kinds

Every stage kind belongs to one lane of the session board. `StageKind::lane` defines the mapping.

| Lane | Stage kinds |
| --- | --- |
| `research` | `Intake`, `Classify`, `Explore`, `Sufficiency`, `Track`, `QuickAnswer`, `Detect`, `Scout` |
| `requirements` | `Spec`, `OpenQuestions`, `Propose`, `SkillApproval` |
| `verification` | `FactCheckSpec`, `FactCheckPlan`, `SpecApproval` |
| `design` | `Stakes`, `Plan`, `PlanApproval` |
| `build` | `Implement`, `Autofix`, `Handoff`, `Rescue`, `Verify`, `PromptGen`, `GenerateSkill`, `GenerateInventory` |
| `review` | `Review`, `Staging`, `Format`, `ImplementationReview` |
| `test` | `ClosingGate`, `Epa`, `WriteTest`, `TestReview` |
| `docs` | `Documentation`, `Architecture`, `BookWrite` |
| `done` | `Completion` |

## Options and added context

`SessionOptions` has four fields: `tests`, `docs`, `yolo`, and `track`. A toggle that is on is an explicit request (Rule T3). The closing gate then skips that question.

A user can add text, files, or uploads to a running session. The engine appends `RequestAmended`. The `delivery` field selects the timing:

- `Queue` (default): executions in progress finish on the old request. The next step sees the new context.
- `Now`: the engine interrupts every execution in progress. Each one runs again with the new context.

After classification, the `RouteAnswer` judge routes added context before any step starts (Rule C2). The limits are `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` (25 MiB), `MAX_UPLOADS` (20), and `MAX_CONTEXT_FILES` (50).

## Pause, resume, and stop

- **Pause (Rule P1).** `Engine::pause_session` appends `SessionPaused` and interrupts executions in progress. A paused session starts nothing, not even a YOLO answer.
- **Resume (Rule P2).** `Engine::resume_session` appends `SessionResumed`. Each interrupted execution continues under its own id.
- **Stop.** `Engine::stop_session` appends `SessionFailed` with the text `Stopped by the user.` It cancels executions in progress and denies waiting permission asks. Work that the session already did stays.
- **Stop when the server is off.** Run `ostra stop <session>`. The next start then does not run the executions again.

## End of a session

The `Completion` judge returns `report_markdown`. The engine writes it to `ostra-completion.md` in the session root and appends `SessionCompleted`. The summary is the first non-empty line of the report. If the judge fails, the engine writes a fallback report that lists the state only.

Completion waits until nothing runs, no created project has an unfinished init, and no subagent question is open (Rule H9). A session also ends with `SessionFailed` when a step returns `Step::Fail`, for example when every research task fails.

An ended session accepts no `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionResumed`, or `CommandStarted` event. `Inner::append` returns `EngineError::Ended` for them. This check runs under the state lock, so a stop cannot race a start.

sections.title: Event log, fold, planner, and runner
sections.summary: Describes how a session is a log of events, how the planner decides the next steps, and how the runner performs them and survives a restart.
sections.body:
A session lasts hours and must survive a restart. It must also be testable without a model. The engine solves both with an append-only event log, a pure planner, and a runner that performs the steps.

## The parts

- **Event log.** Each session has a list of `SessionEvent` values in the `events` table of `workspace.db`. The key is `(session_id, seq)`.
- **Fold.** `SessionState::fold` reads the events in order and builds `SessionState`. The fold is deterministic: the same events always give the same state. For this reason a restart can replay the log and continue.
- **Planner.** `next_steps(state, ctx)` is a pure function. It returns a list of `Step` values. It reads no clock, no disk, and no network.
- **Runner.** `Engine` in `runner.rs` performs each step and appends the resulting events.

## Step kinds

| `Step` | What the runner does |
| --- | --- |
| `Judge` | Calls a judge and appends `DecisionMade`. |
| `Spawn` | Starts an agent execution. |
| `OpenGate` | Appends `GateOpened`. |
| `YoloAnswer` | Answers a gate under YOLO. |
| `Command` | Runs the format or stage command of a project. |
| `Autofix` | Applies mechanical review fixes. |
| `AnnounceBlocked` | Appends `PhaseBlocked`. |
| `FinishInit`, `RecordInitProblem` | End or fail the init of a created project. |
| `Deliver` | Hands a message to a harness execution that waits. |
| `WriteBook` | Writes the documentation book. |
| `Complete`, `Fail` | End the session. |

## The driver loop

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Driver as drive loop
    participant Planner as next_steps
    participant State as SessionState
    participant Perform as perform
    participant Store as workspace.db
    Driver->>State: read state under lock
    Driver->>Planner: next_steps
    Planner-->>Driver: steps
    Driver->>Perform: spawn a task per new step key
    Perform->>Store: append event
    Perform->>State: apply stored event
    Perform-->>Driver: wake
    Driver->>Planner: next_steps again
```

`Inner::ensure_driver` starts one driver task for each session. The driver computes the steps and starts a task for each step. Each step has a key from `Step::key`. The driver keeps the keys of steps in flight in the `inflight` set, so it never starts one step twice. When a step task ends, it removes its key and wakes the driver. The driver then plans again.

If a step fails with an error other than `EngineError::Ended`, the driver appends a `Note` with the text `A step failed: ...` and goes on.

## What append does

`Inner::append` is the only way to add an event. It does these actions in order, under the state lock of the session:

1. Refuse start events when the session already ended.
2. Store the event in `workspace.db`.
3. Materialize the event into the tables for the UI (`materialize`).
4. Apply the event to the in-memory `SessionState`.
5. Update the session row: category, status, lane, stage label, projects, cost, and title.
6. Broadcast `EngineNotice::SessionUpdated` and `EngineNotice::Event`.
7. Ask for a push notice (`push_for`) and wake the driver.

The lock serializes appends for one session. Therefore the order of `seq` is the order of the fold.

## Planner filters

`Planner::push` drops or changes a step before it reaches the list. These rules apply:

- A created project that awaits its init accepts only the `initializer` and `advisor` agents (Rule O4). Other agents route their work by the inventory and the profile of the project.
- A spawn for an execution that waits for a message is held. The message wakes the execution in place (Rule H2).
- A spawn that replaces a paused execution resumes that execution (Rule P2).
- A pair loop continues the conversation of the execution before it (Rules H5 and H6). One conversation has one live execution (Rule H7).
- The budget guard blocks new spawns after the budget is spent. See the page Execution lifecycle, slots, and budget.

## Restart recovery

`Engine::recover` runs at server start for every session of the workspace:

1. Each execution that was running gets an `ExecutionFinished` event. The status is `Interrupted` with the error `The server restarted while this execution ran.` A harness execution that waited for a message gets the status `Waiting`.
2. Each open `Permission` gate gets a `Deny` answer, because the execution that asked is gone.
3. Each loop that was in flight runs its work again with `WorkKind::Rerun`.
4. The engine starts the driver for each session that is not terminal.

Usage that the executions already spent stays, because the engine stores usage deltas while the executions run.

## Event catalog

| Group | Events |
| --- | --- |
| Session | `SessionCreated`, `RequestAmended`, `SessionPaused`, `SessionResumed`, `YoloSet`, `SessionCompleted`, `SessionFailed`, `Note` |
| Executions | `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionResumed`, `ExecutionFinished`, `ContainmentSignal` |
| Messages between agents | `AgentAsked`, `AgentReplied`, `MessageDelivered` |
| Judges | `DecisionMade`, `DecisionOverridden` |
| Gates | `GateOpened`, `GateAnswered` |
| Commands | `CommandStarted`, `CommandRan`, `AutofixApplied` |
| Review | `SecurityBlock`, `PhaseBlocked` |
| Projects | `ProjectCreated`, `ProjectInitFinished`, `InitStepFailed` |
| Books | `BookWritten` |

## Rules for a change

Old logs must still parse. The code follows three habits:

- A new field on an existing event has `#[serde(default)]`.
- A renamed name keeps an alias. Examples: `module-docs` for `Documentation`, `UNIT_TEST` for `Test`, `module_docs` for `ExecPurpose::Docs`.
- The fold reads only the events. Do not read the clock, the disk, or the environment in `SessionState::apply`, because a replay must give the same state.

The conformance tests in `tests/conformance/main.rs` build an event history, fold it, and check the steps. Add a fixture there for each new planner rule.

sections.title: Research, spec, and plan stages
sections.summary: Describes the explore tasks, the spec flow with fact-check and approval, the stakes check, and the plan flow that precede code on the full track.
sections.body:
Code written from a guess breaks. On the full track, the pipeline first collects facts, then fixes the requirements in a spec, then orders the work in a plan. A `fact-check` agent must pass each document before the user sees it.

## Explore tasks and sufficiency

The `Classify` judge returns explore tasks. A task has a project and a text. The planner starts every ready explore at once, because explore is read-only (Rule M1). The number of parallel executions stays under `limits.max_parallel_executions`.

Each explore execution writes one research document with the `Document` tool. The document has a list of `Not covered` items.

After all tasks finish, the planner checks for unjudged `Not covered` items. If any exist, it returns a `Sufficiency` judge step. The judge can queue more explore tasks. The engine runs at most `SUFFICIENCY_ROUNDS` (3) rounds. After that, it goes on with the research that it has.

If no research document exists, the session fails. This is Rule D1. The error text is `Every research task failed or was abandoned, so there is no research document to write a spec from.`

Each explore task has an origin. `Rescue`, `LoopAnswer`, and `Ask` tasks are loop-bound: only the work loop or the asker waits for them. Other origins hold the whole session.

## Spec flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Run[generate-spec writes the spec] --> Q{Open questions}
    Q -->|yes| QG[OpenQuestions gate]
    QG --> Run
    Q -->|no| FC[fact-check pass]
    FC --> V{Verdict}
    V -->|Fail| Count{3 fails in a row}
    Count -->|no| Run
    Count -->|yes| RG[FactCheckRecurring gate]
    RG -->|another round| Run
    V -->|Pass| Need{Approval needed}
    Need -->|no| Done[Spec done]
    Need -->|yes| AG[SpecApproval gate]
    AG -->|changes| Run
    AG -->|approved| Done
```

The steps in order:

1. `generate-spec` reads every research document and writes one spec with the `Document` tool.
2. If the spec has open questions that were not asked for this version, the planner opens an `OpenQuestions` gate before any fact-check (Rule D3). The engine writes each answer back into the spec.
3. `fact-check` checks the spec. The `source_check` input is `refetch` only on the first pass of a spec that has External Evidence rows. Otherwise it is `citations` (Rule D3b).
4. The verdict is `Pass`, `Fail`, or `Error`. After `Fail`, `generate-spec` rewrites the spec in place with the findings. The file name stays the same, so the next pass compares against its snapshot (Rule D3a).
5. After `FACTCHECK_RECURRING_LIMIT` (3) consecutive fails, plus `fail_limit_extra`, the planner opens a `FactCheckRecurring` gate.
6. Only the categories `PLAN` and `IMPLEMENT` (full track) need approval. The planner opens `SpecApproval` for them.

The engine refuses an approval without a `Pass` for the current version. `Engine::answer_gate` returns `Approval requires a fact-check PASS on this version.` A change to the spec revokes the approval.

## Stakes and plan flow

After the spec is approved on the full track, the `Stakes` judge rates the work.

| Stakes | Meaning | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `low` | One deliverable in one project, easy to revert, no schema or contract change. | The plan stage is skipped. The implementer works from the spec in one inline phase for each project. |
| `medium` | Several files in one area, a changed contract, a new integration point, or more than one deliverable. | The plan stage runs. |
| `high` | An architecture change, a migration, a cross-project change, or a shared library change. | The plan stage runs. |

The judge prompt resolves any doubt upward, because a skipped plan removes the phase review that catches a wrong order.

The `plan` agent reads the spec and its own earlier plan, and nothing else (Rule D4). A `Fail` verdict adds findings (Rule D5). The plan fact-check always uses `citations`.

The plan holds a master plan and one file for each phase. A phase (`PhaseInfo`) has these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `title`, `deliverable` | Identity and purpose. |
| `project` | The project key. A key that does not exist yet means the phase creates that project. |
| `complexity` | `Low`, `Medium`, or `High`. It routes the model tier of `implementer` and `write-test`. |
| `test_policy` | `Required` (default) or `Skip` with a rationale. Any doubt means `Required` (Rule T4). |
| `depends_on` | Phase ids. `None` means unreadable and counts as a dependency on every earlier phase (Rule M5). |
| `file` | The phase file. An inline phase has none. |

## Changes after approval

A plan question changes requirements. The answer goes into the spec first, then the plan is written again (Rule D10). The plan is `invalidated` when the spec changes, and the `plan` agent revises it against the spec diff.

The engine holds a free-text answer to a spec or plan gate until the `RouteAnswer` judge decides where it goes. See the page Gates and answers.

## Failures

- If an execution of this stage ends in error, the engine retries it once (`ERROR_RETRIES`). Then it opens an `ExecutionFailed` gate. A harness that cannot start opens a `HarnessFailure` gate.
- If the user stops the stage, the planner returns `Step::Fail` with `The spec stage was stopped.` or the same text for the plan.
- YOLO never retries an execution that the user stopped (Rule P4).

sections.title: Work loops and the review cycle
sections.summary: Explains the implement and test loops, the review cap, severities, auto-fix, rescue, handoff, and blocked phases.
sections.body:
One agent pass seldom gives acceptable code. A work loop pairs a work agent with the `code-reviewer` agent. It repeats until no HIGH or MEDIUM finding remains or a cap stops it. This page explains the loop, its limits, and every way it can end.

## Loop kinds

Each phase (`PhaseRun`) has two loops and one analysis state:

- `impl_loop`: the work agent is `implementer`. For a `VERIFY` request the same agent runs the project test command. For a `PROMPT` request the work agent is `prompt-generation`.
- `test_loop`: the work agent is `write-test`. It runs in the closing stages.
- `epa`: the execution-path analysis that feeds `write-test`.

The reviewer gets a `Phase:` value of `N` for an implement loop and `N-tests` for a test loop. Each loop has a review ledger, `ostra-review-ledger-phase-<value>.md`. The reviewer and the work agent both write it.

## States of a loop

`WorkLoop.next` holds a `LoopNext` value. The planner reads it and returns the next step.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Work: dependencies passed
    Work --> Review: submit ok
    Work --> Rescue: submit stuck
    Work --> Handoff: submit handoff
    Work --> Failed: error after one retry
    Handoff --> Work: resume after prompt-generation
    Rescue --> Work: rerun with a fact
    Rescue --> RescueExplore: research the fact
    Rescue --> RescueGate: ask the user
    Review --> Work: fix HIGH or MEDIUM
    Review --> Work: blocker fix
    Review --> Autofix: auto-fixable findings
    Autofix --> Work: remaining findings
    Review --> Stage: no finding left
    Review --> CapReached: cap reached
    CapReached --> Work: another pass
    CapReached --> Blocked: stop
    Stage --> Done: git add finished
```

## Review findings

The reviewer returns findings with a severity: `BLOCKER`, `HIGH`, `MEDIUM`, or `LOW`.

| Severity | What the loop does |
| --- | --- |
| `BLOCKER` | A non-waivable security finding. The finding goes alone to the fix agent as a `BlockerFix` with an instruction to remove the dangerous code. No cap applies. `blocker_open` stays true until a review has none. An open blocker stops the docs stage (hard rule 21). |
| `HIGH`, `MEDIUM` | The fix agent gets these findings verbatim and the ledger path. The agent records `FIXED` or `WONTFIX` with a reason for each. |
| `LOW` | The engine keeps them in `leftover_low`. No fix runs for them. |

A finding whose rule has `auto_fixable = true` in `project.toml` goes to `Step::Autofix`. The engine applies its exact `Fix:` text, for example a line that says to change one quoted text to another on line N. The rules `SEC-BLOCK*` and `PHASE-REQ*` are never auto-fixable. A finding that the engine cannot apply goes back to the fix agent.

## Caps

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `REVIEW_CAP` | 3 | Review passes before the fourth becomes a gate. |
| `YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET` | 10 | Review passes under YOLO. |
| `extra_cap` | grows | The user adds passes with the answer `another-pass`. |
| `ERROR_RETRIES` | 1 | Automatic retries of an execution that ends in error. |
| `MAX_ANSWER_RESEARCH` | 3 | Research tasks that one answer can queue. |

When the cap is reached and YOLO is off, the planner opens a `ReviewCap` gate. The user answers `another-pass` or `stop`. When YOLO is on, the `ResolveReview` judge decides `Fix` or `Block`. The engine repeats a resolution round only while the number of open findings falls. If the number does not fall, the phase becomes `Blocked` with the text `The review loop stopped converging`.

## Stuck and handoff

An agent submits `status: stuck` with a `diagnostic` and a `need`. The `Rescue` judge picks one of three actions:

- `Explore`: queue a research task for the missing fact. The loop waits for it.
- `Rerun`: run the work again with a stated fact (`WorkKind::Rescue`).
- `Gate`: open a `Stuck` gate so the user states the fact or leaves the phase blocked.

An agent submits `status: handoff` when it needs a specialist. The planner starts `prompt-generation` with the handoff request. After it finishes, the work agent resumes (`WorkKind::Resume`).

## Blocked phases

A blocked phase announces itself with `PhaseBlocked`. Phases that depend on it leave the queue. Independent phases keep running (Rule D9). Without YOLO, a `PhaseBlocked` gate asks the user to retry with instructions or leave the phase blocked.

## Scheduling

One implement pipeline runs for each project at a time (Rule M2). A phase starts when all its dependencies pass. Test loops run one phase at a time in phase order. The analysis runs in parallel for all covered phases.

## When the code is done

After the last phase of a project, the planner opens the `ImplementationReview` gate (Rule F1). The user tries the result. The user answers `done`, or `feedback` with text. The `Feedback` judge routes each feedback round, and the engine builds a revision phase. A revision reads the session context file `ostra-session-context.md`, not a conversation (Rule F2).

sections.title: Format, tests, documentation, and books
sections.summary: Describes the closing stages after code is done: format, the closing gate, tests, the docs stage, and how the engine writes and merges a documentation book.
sections.body:
After the code of a project passes review, three optional jobs remain: format the code, write tests, and write documentation. Tests and documentation cost executions, so the user chooses. This page covers the closing stages and the book that the docs stage produces.

## Format

The planner runs the format command once for each project after its last phase (Rule D8). The command comes from `[commands] format` in `.ostra/project.toml`. The step is not gated. If the command changed outside Ostra and is not approved, the engine skips it and records `FORMAT_NOT_APPROVED`.

## Closing gate

The planner opens one `ClosingGate` for all projects that reach it together (Rule T6). Each item has `ask_tests` and `ask_docs`. An option that the request already set (`tests` or `docs`) is not asked (Rule T3). Under YOLO the gate answers no tests and no docs, unless the request asked for them.

## Test stage

The closing gate answer `tests` starts the test stage for a project:

1. The engine selects the covered phases: phases with no plan file, and phases with `test_policy = Required` (Rule T4).
2. The `execution-path-analyzer` agent runs for each covered phase, in parallel. It writes an EPA report `ostra-epa-phase-<N>.md`.
3. The `write-test` agent runs for one phase at a time, in phase order. It uses the EPA report. A review loop follows each pass (`test_loop`).
4. A failed analysis opens an `ExecutionFailed` gate. An abandoned analysis skips its phase.

A `TEST` request with no implementer gets a stub report `ostra-test-request.md` from the engine. The stub names the request as the code under test.

## Docs stage

The `documentation` agent runs once for each project (Rule B1). It gets the implementer reports of the passed phases. An open `BLOCKER` stops it. At most `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` (4) writers run at once (Rule B7).

For a `DOCS` request no implementer ran. The engine writes the stub `ostra-docs-request.md`. It holds the request and says that no file changed.

When two or more parts exist, the `system-architecture` agent runs after the parts. It reads `ostra-docs-parts.json`, which the engine writes from the submitted parts (Rule B4). Then the planner returns `Step::WriteBook`.

Agents write no book file. The guard `workspace-docs` refuses a write under the books folder (Rule B5). Each agent returns its part in its submit call. The engine validates the submit before it accepts it. `check_documentation` requires at least one section, unique slug ids, valid diagram sizes, and valid glossary entries.

## Book storage

The book lives in `<workspace>/.ostra/docs/<book id>/`:

| File | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `book.json` | The whole book as JSON. |
| `index.md` | The index of the book. |
| `glossary.md` | The merged glossary. |
| `architecture.md` | The system architecture, when two or more parts exist. |
| `<project>/<section>.md` | One file for each section of a part. |

`book::write` removes files of sections that no longer exist.

### Book identity and merge

- The book id is the sorted project keys joined by `_` (Rule B6). A later session on the same projects updates the same book. An id longer than `MAX_BOOK_ID` (80 characters) is cut and gets a 16-digit hash suffix. The user can pick an existing book in the new task form (`docs_book`).
- A new part replaces the old part of the same project. A new architecture replaces the old one. Glossary entries merge by term, and the newer definition wins.
- `BOOK_LOCK` serializes each read, merge, and write. Therefore two sessions that update one book keep each other's parts.
- If the write fails, the engine records `BookWritten` with an `error` and the session goes on.

### Diagram limits

`check_diagram` refuses a sequence diagram with more than `MAX_SEQUENCE_PARTICIPANTS` (8) participants or `MAX_SEQUENCE_MESSAGES` (20) messages. It refuses a flowchart with more than `MAX_FLOWCHART_NODES` (15) nodes.

## Search by agents

Agents with the `docs_search` capability read books with `DocsSearch` (Rule B8). The search cuts each section into small passages and ranks them with BM25 over title, code, and body fields. The default limit is `DEFAULT_LIMIT` (5) hits and the maximum is `MAX_LIMIT` (15). A hit shows at most `PASSAGES_PER_HIT` (2) passages. A fact that appears on many pages returns many hits, so write each fact once.

sections.title: Gates and answers
sections.summary: Lists every gate kind with its answers and its YOLO behavior, and explains how the engine validates and routes an answer.
sections.body:
A pipeline needs facts and decisions that only the user has. A gate is a record that waits for an answer. The engine opens a gate with `GateOpened`. The user answers through the console, and the engine appends `GateAnswered`. This page lists the gate kinds and the rules for answers.

## Gate catalog

`GatePayload` defines the kinds. `kind_str` gives the name that the API uses.

| Kind | Opens when | Answer | Under YOLO |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `open_questions` | A spec or plan has questions. | `Questions` with one non-empty answer for each question id. | A judge answers. A missing answer takes the recommended option. |
| `spec_approval` | The spec passed fact-check. | `Approval {approved, feedback}`. A rejection needs feedback. | A judge answers. It can approve only after a `Pass`. |
| `plan_approval` | The plan passed fact-check. | Like the spec. | Like the spec. |
| `fact_check_recurring` | 3 fails in a row. | `Choice`: `another-round` or `stop`, with optional guidance text. | `another-round` while fewer than 6 fails. Then `stop`. |
| `review_cap` | A loop reached its cap. | `Choice`: `another-pass` or `stop`. | The loop uses the `ResolveReview` judge instead. |
| `stuck` | An agent reported `stuck`. | `Choice`: `fact` with text, or `block`. | A judge answers. A `fact` without text becomes `block`. |
| `phase_blocked` | A phase ended blocked. | `Choice`: `retry` or `leave`. | `leave`. |
| `closing_gate` | Code is done. | `Closing` with `tests` and `docs` for each project. | Defaults: no tests and no docs, unless requested. |
| `permission` | A tool call needs an answer. | `AllowOnce`, `AlwaysInWorkspace`, or `Deny`. | `AllowOnce`. |
| `harness_failure` | A harness CLI cannot start or is not signed in. | `Choice`: `retry` or `native`. | `native`. |
| `skill_approval` | An init proposed skills. | `Skills` with a disposition for each skill. | The proposed defaults. |
| `execution_failed` | An execution failed after its retry. | `Choice`: `retry` or `abandon`. | `retry` twice for one agent, then `abandon`. Never for an execution that the user stopped. |
| `implementation_review` | Every phase finished. | `Choice`: `done`, or `feedback` with text. | `done`. |
| `budget_reached` | The session spent its budget. | `Choice`: `raise` with dollars in `text`, or `stop`. | Never answered. |

## Rules for an answer

`Engine::answer_gate` checks an answer before it appends the event:

1. The gate must have no answer. Otherwise the error is `This gate was already answered.`
2. The answer shape must fit the gate. `validate_answer` returns `That answer does not fit this gate.` for a mismatch.
3. A spec or plan approval needs a `Pass` for the current version.
4. The answer `AlwaysInWorkspace` adds the suggested rule (`suggest_rule`) to the `permissions.allow` list of the workspace.

The event `GateAnswered` records the `source`: `User`, `Yolo`, or `Engine`. The engine uses `Engine` for answers that need no judgment, for example a permission ask of an execution that ended.

## Routing of free-text answers (Rule J1)

A bare choice has one meaning, so the engine applies it at once. A free-text answer can change requirements, so it waits for the `RouteAnswer` judge. `answer_needs_route` marks these answers with `routed: true`:

- `Questions` with at least one answer.
- An approval with feedback text.
- `fact_check_recurring` with any option but `stop` and with text.
- `another-pass`, `fact`, `retry`, and `feedback` answers that carry text.

The judge returns a route and one item for each answer.

| `AnswerRoute` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `RequirementChange` | The answer changes requirements. It goes into the spec first. |
| `ImplementationDetail` | The answer guides the current stage. |
| `StageChoice` | The answer picks an option of the stage. |

| `Disposition` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Deliver` | The current stage acts on the answer now. |
| `Remember` | The engine keeps a note for later stages (`Implement`, `Tests`, `Docs`). |
| `Discard` | The engine drops the answer. The gate answer stays in the log. |

The judge can also queue up to `MAX_ANSWER_RESEARCH` (3) research tasks that run before the answer applies. It can also name earlier notes to forget. A note that the judge keeps reaches the spawn block of a later stage as `User notes`.

When the judge returns nothing for an item, the engine delivers the answer, because the user gave it.

## Permission gates

A permission ask comes from a live execution, not from the planner. `EngineHost::ask_permission` opens the gate and waits on a channel. The answer, a stop, or a pause ends the wait. A stop or an interrupt answers `Deny` for each waiting ask. If YOLO turns on when an ask waits, the engine answers it with `AllowOnce` at once.

## Budget gate

The planner opens `budget_reached` once when the spent amount reaches the limit. Executions in progress finish. New spawns wait. If the user answers `raise`, the engine adds the dollars to `budget_raised`. YOLO never raises a budget, because spending more is the decision of the user.

sections.title: Judges and YOLO
sections.summary: Lists the ten judge kinds, explains how a judge call runs, fails, and is overridden, and explains what YOLO changes.
sections.body:
The pipeline code must not guess where a decision needs judgment. A judge is a single model call that returns JSON against a schema. It is the only place where a model makes an orchestration decision. The engine stores each result as a `DecisionMade` event with a reason.

## Judge catalog

| `JudgeKind` | Question | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Classify` | Which category, projects, and first research tasks? | `ClassifyOut` |
| `Sufficiency` | Does each `Not covered` item need more research? | `SufficiencyOut` |
| `Track` | Light or full track for an `IMPLEMENT` request? | `TrackOut` |
| `Stakes` | `low`, `medium`, or `high`? | `StakesOut` |
| `RouteAnswer` | Where does a free-text answer or added context go? | `RouteAnswerOut` |
| `Feedback` | Which projects does a feedback round change, and with what instruction? | `FeedbackOut` (needs at least one target) |
| `Rescue` | How to continue after an agent reported `stuck`? | `RescueOut` |
| `ResolveReview` | At the review cap under YOLO: fix or block? | `ResolveReviewOut` |
| `YoloAnswer` | What answer fits this gate? | `YoloAnswerOut` |
| `Completion` | What does the final report say? | `CompletionOut` |

Each judge has a prompt in `assets/judges/<name>.md`. The file name matches `JudgeKind::as_str`, for example `route-answer.md`.

## How a call runs

`Inner::call_judge` does these steps:

1. Load the prompt from the spawn factory.
2. Resolve the route with the key `judge` and the default tier `advanced`. The judge always runs on the native path with an API key. It never runs in a harness, because `Services::judge` calls `ostra_providers::structured`.
3. Call the provider with the effort `Low`. The model must call a tool named `decide` whose input matches the schema.
4. Check the output against the Rust type of the judge. A bad shape counts as a failed attempt.
5. Retry up to 3 attempts in total. The delay is 500 ms times the attempt number.
6. Append `DecisionMade` and add the usage to the judge cost of the session.

If all attempts fail, the engine appends `SessionFailed` with the error and the hint `Check that the judge route has a provider with a working API key.` The `Completion` judge is the exception. Its failure gives a fallback report that lists the state, because the work is done.

The judge cost counts toward the cost that the session list shows. The budget guard does not count it, because the guard sums the cost of finished executions only.

## Override

`Engine::override_decision` lets the user replace a decision. It works only for `Classify`, `Stakes`, `Track`, and `Sufficiency`. It works only before dependent work starts (`can_override`). The new output must match the output type of the judge. The engine appends `DecisionOverridden`.

## YOLO

YOLO is a per-session switch. A workspace sets the default with `yolo.default`. The user toggles it with `Engine::set_yolo`, which appends `YoloSet`. YOLO changes three behaviors:

- **Gates.** The planner returns a `YoloAnswer` step for each open gate. Two groups are exceptions: `permission` gates, and the gates that `yolo_leaves_open` names (`budget_reached`, and `execution_failed` for an execution that the user stopped). `YoloPlan::Fixed` gives a fixed answer. `YoloPlan::Judge` asks the `YoloAnswer` judge. See the page Gates and answers for each kind.
- **Permissions.** Layer 2 of the policy turns each `Ask` into an `Allow` with the rule `yolo`. Layer 1 guards and `Deny` results still apply.
- **Review cap.** The loop budget is 10 passes, and the `ResolveReview` judge resolves the cap.

The engine enforces what must stay true when a judge answers a gate. `yolo_answer_from_judge` accepts an approval only after a fact-check `Pass`. It requires feedback for a rejection. It fills each missing question with the recommended option. If the judge fails, the engine appends a `Note` and the gate waits for the user.

A paused session starts nothing, not even a YOLO answer (Rule P1).

sections.title: Execution lifecycle, slots, and budget
sections.summary: Follows one agent execution from spawn to finish: slots, route resolution, context, status values, pause and resume, containment, timeouts, and the session budget.
sections.body:
The planner asks for an agent. The runner must pick a model, build the prompt, limit parallel work, run the agent, and record the result. `Inner::perform_spawn` does this. An execution is one run of one agent.

## Steps of a spawn

1. **Wait for a slot.** `acquire_slot` waits until the count of running executions is under the limit.
2. **Check the session.** A terminal or paused session starts nothing.
3. **Find an execution to continue.** A paused execution (status `Interrupted` or `Waiting`) resumes under its own id. A pair loop can instead continue the conversation of an earlier execution (Rules H3 and H5).
4. **Resolve the route.** `resolve_route` picks the executor and the model. A continued execution keeps its executor and model, which also keeps the prompt cache.
5. **Find the executor.** If none exists, the runner records a `Denied` execution with the reason.
6. **Pick the repo root.** It is the project path. A phase in a project that does not exist yet runs from its session dir (Rule O2).
7. **Load project facts.** The runner reads `project.toml`, `INVENTORY.md`, and the project instruction files.
8. **Build the spawn.** `SpawnFactory::build` returns the system prompt, the first message, the spawn block, the params, the report file, and the effort.
9. **Build `ExecContext`.** It holds the roots, the permission rules, the sandbox settings, the protected paths, and the YOLO flag.
10. **Record the start.** The runner appends `ExecutionStarted` (or `ExecutionResumed`) and inserts the execution row.
11. **Run.** `Executor::run(spec, host, token)` returns an `ExecutionResult`.
12. **Record the end.** The runner adds usage, maps a cancel to `Interrupted` when the session interrupted the execution, stores the result, and appends `ExecutionFinished`.

If route resolution or the spawn build fails, the runner records the execution as `Denied` with the text `route: ...` or `spawn: ...`.

## Slots

The limit is `limits.max_parallel_executions` (default 3, minimum 1). A `Slot` value gives the slot back in its `Drop` and wakes the waiters. Therefore the slot returns after success, failure, cancel, or a panic.

A waiting spawn checks again when a slot frees and at least every 2 seconds. It reads the limit from the settings each time. If you raise the limit, waiting spawns start within 2 seconds, with no restart. If you lower the limit, nothing is cancelled. Executions that already run finish, and new ones wait until the count is under the new limit.

- **Holds a slot:** each agent execution of a session, on every executor. The limit is for each workspace, so two sessions of one workspace share it.
- **Gives its slot back when it waits:** an execution that waits for a message from another subagent (Rule H2). It takes a slot again before it receives the message. Without this rule, a limit of 1 blocks: the waiting execution holds the only slot, and the execution that it waits for cannot start.
- **Holds no slot:** judge calls. They are short and do not go through `perform_spawn`.

## Execution statuses

| `ExecutionStatus` | Meaning | What the fold does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Running` | The execution runs. | Nothing. |
| `Ok` | The agent submitted a result. | The stage uses the submit. |
| `Stuck` | The agent submitted `status: stuck`. | A work loop goes to rescue. |
| `Handoff` | The agent asked for a specialist. | A work loop goes to handoff. |
| `Waiting` | The execution waits for a message from a subagent. | It resumes in place when the message comes. |
| `Error` | The execution failed. | One automatic retry, then an `ExecutionFailed` gate. A `harness-` error opens a `HarnessFailure` gate at once. |
| `Denied` | The runner could not start it. | The stage treats it as a failure. |
| `Interrupted` | A pause, a context change, a project creation, or a restart stopped it. | It runs again from its progress. |
| `Cancelled` | A stop or a user cancel ended it. | A user cancel opens an `ExecutionFailed` gate titled `You stopped <agent>`. YOLO leaves that gate open. |

The three interrupt reasons (`Interrupt`) are `Pause`, `Context`, and `ProjectCreated`.

## Timeouts

Each agent has `timeout_seconds` in its `agent.toml`. The native executor ends an execution with the error `timed out after N s`. The harness executor uses the larger of the value and 30 seconds. Time that a harness execution spends in a wait for a message does not count.

## Containment pause

The runner records each containment signal as an event, at most `PAUSE_AFTER` (3) for one execution. The third signal pauses the session (Rule P3). A signal is a refusal by the guards `secret-read`, `self-protection`, or `git-metadata`, a refused connection to a local address, or a read of a decoy credential file. See the page Sandbox, egress proxy, and decoys.

## Session budget

The setting `limits.session_budget_usd` has the default 25.0. The value 0 means no limit. The spent amount is the sum of `cost_usd` of finished executions. When the spent amount reaches the limit plus `budget_raised`, `Planner::push` drops every new spawn and opens one `budget_reached` gate. Executions in progress finish. If the user raises the budget, new spawns start again.

## Side effects of a spawn

- The planner never starts a second spawn for a purpose that is in flight, because `Step::key` dedupes it.
- The runner removes the tool cache of a session when it ends (`remove_session_cache`).
- The runner writes `ostra-session-context.md` before a revision or an implementation review reads it.

sections.title: Subagent coordination
sections.summary: Explains how agents ask each other questions, how a waiting execution wakes, and the limits on helpers and messages.
sections.body:
A reviewer or a spec writer often needs a fact from the agent that wrote the earlier artifact. A cold read of a report loses context. Subagent coordination lets one agent ask another and continue with the answer. This page covers the tools, the routes, and the limits.

## Subagents and IDs

A subagent is one conversation. Its subagent ID is the id of the first execution of that conversation. A later execution that continues the conversation has the same subagent ID.

Agents with the `coordinate` capability get three tools:

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `SubagentList` | Lists the subagents of the session with agent, status, and report. |
| `SubagentAsk` | Sends a question. The target is a new helper (`agent`) or an existing subagent (`subagent_id`). Give exactly one. |
| `SubagentReply` | Answers a question that woke this execution. |

The agents with this capability are `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `implementer`, `code-reviewer`, and `write-test`. On a harness the tools come from the `ostra` MCP server.

## Routes of a question

`SessionState::route` picks the route for a question to a subagent:

| `Route` | When | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WakeInPlace` | The subagent waits on the asker. | The engine wakes it with the question. |
| `Consult` | The subagent ended its execution. | The planner starts a consult execution (`ExecPurpose::Consult`) that continues the subagent conversation. |
| `Pending` | The subagent is busy. | The question waits. |
| `Failed` | The target is invalid. | The asker gets the failure as its answer. |

A question to `explore` starts a helper research task with the origin `Ask`. The only helper agent is `explore` (`HELPER_AGENTS`). A helper failure is the answer to the asker, not a gate (Rule H3).

A consult execution answers from its conversation. It writes no file (`answer_only`) and must call `SubagentReply` before it ends (`owes_reply`). The guards enforce both rules.

## How a waiting execution wakes

1. The asker calls `SubagentAsk`. The engine appends `AgentAsked`.
2. The tool result tells the asker to end its turn. The execution status becomes `Waiting`.
3. The waiting execution gives its slot back.
4. When the answer exists, the planner returns `Step::Deliver` for a harness execution, or a spawn that resumes the execution for a native one.
5. The engine appends `MessageDelivered`, and the executor feeds the answer as the next message.

A harness process stays alive during the wait, and the wait does not count against its timeout. A native execution stops, and its stored transcript rebuilds the conversation.

## Limits

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_HELPERS_PER_RUN` | 3 | Helpers that one execution can start (Rule H4). |
| `MAX_SESSION_ASKS` | 24 | Questions that one session can ask (Rule H4). |
| `MAX_CONVERSATION_RUNS` | 6 | Executions of one conversation before a pair loop starts fresh (Rule H6). |
| `MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS` | 8000 | Length of one question or answer. |

Put longer material in a file and name its path in the message.

## Continued conversations

A pair loop continues the conversation of the earlier execution (Rules H5 and H6). Examples are fact-check findings that go back to the spec writer, and review findings that go back to the implementer. The continued execution gets a new spawn block with `continuation_note`. One conversation has one live execution (Rule H7). Completion waits when any subagent question is open (Rule H9).

The `coordination.md` guide in `assets/` tells each agent when to ask: only when the answer saves real work, with a question that stands alone.

sections.body:
Each stage needs an agent with the right role, tools, and model tier. The agents live in `assets/agents/<name>/`. `AgentName` lists them, and the names are the folder names. This page covers the agent catalog and how the engine turns an agent into a first message.

## Agent catalog

| Agent | Role | Default tier | Timeout (s) | Writes project source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | Researches one task and writes one research document. The only agent that searches the web for the pipeline. | advanced | 1800 | No |
| `generate-spec` | Reads all research and writes one spec in EARS notation. | advanced | 1800 | No |
| `fact-check` | Checks a spec or plan and returns a verdict with findings. | advanced | 1800 | No |
| `plan` | Turns an approved spec into a master plan and phase files. | advanced | 1800 | No |
| `implementer` | Writes the code of one phase. Never writes tests. | balanced | 2400 | Yes |
| `code-reviewer` | Reviews working-tree changes and runs a security scan. | balanced | 1200 | No |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Plans test checks from the paths through changed code. | balanced | 1200 | No |
| `write-test` | Writes only test code and runs the suites. | balanced | 2400 | Yes (tests) |
| `documentation` | Writes one project part of a book. | advanced | 2400 | No |
| `system-architecture` | Writes the architecture of a book of two or more projects. | advanced | 1800 | No |
| `prompt-generation` | Writes prompts, skills, and agent files. | advanced | 1800 | Yes |
| `initializer` | Bootstraps a project: detect, scout, propose, generate skills, generate inventory, adopt. | balanced | 2400 | Yes (`.ostra`, skills) |
| `quick-answer` | Answers one question in the side panel. Read-only. | balanced | 300 | No |
| `advisor` | Reads a failed step and tells the engine how to continue. | advanced | 900 | No |

`AgentName::is_session_only` lists the agents that write only in their session dir and the OS temp dir: `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `advisor`, `documentation`, and `system-architecture`. Seeded workspace routes override the default tiers. See the page Settings, routing, and project profiles.

Every agent uses the effort `high`, with these exceptions: `quick-answer` uses `medium`, and `initializer` uses `xhigh` on Codex and Grok and `max` on Antigravity.

## The assets folder

| Path | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `agents/<name>/agent.toml` | Description, `default_tier`, `timeout_seconds`, `capabilities`, and `effort` for each executor table. |
| `agents/<name>/prompt.md` | The prompt, as a MiniJinja template. |
| `judges/<name>.md` | Judge prompts. |
| `refs/*.md` | Stack references (`java-spring`, `go`, `python`, `typescript-node`, `_generic`) and two guides. |
| `skills/meta-author/SKILL.md` | The skill that ships with Ostra. |
| `tool-mapping.toml` | The tool name of each capability on each executor. |
| `output-rules.md`, `code-tools.md`, `coordination.md` | Preludes that the renderer adds to prompts. |

`ostra-agents` embeds the folder at compile time. At server start, `materialize_assets` writes the references, the skills, and each agent prompt (rendered for the native executor) under `<data dir>/assets`. The `advisor` reads those files to learn what a failed step can do. A broken `agent.toml` panics at first use with `embedded agent definitions are invalid`.

## Prompt rendering

`render_prompt(agent, executor)` builds the system prompt in this order:

1. For a harness executor, a tool vocabulary section from `tool-mapping.toml`.
2. `output-rules.md`: write no text outside tool calls, and put the result in the submit call.
3. The coordination guide, when the agent has `coordinate`.
4. The code navigation guide, when the agent has `code`.
5. The prompt of the agent.

The renderer treats a missing template variable as an error. `tool-mapping.toml` has one table for each executor: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. Native names follow Claude Code, because the prompts are tuned to them.

## Spawn block and repo brief

The planner makes a `SpawnRequest`. `AgentsFactory::build` turns it into typed `SpawnParams` and renders a `Label: value` block, the spawn block. It starts with `Workspace root`, `Repo root`, `Session dir`, and `Repo key`. Other lines name phase files, research documents, findings, report files, and user notes.

The first message has three parts after the spawn block:

1. **Repo brief.** At most `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` (3600) characters with the stack, the exact commands, test types, up to 16 skills, conventions, and up to 10 module rows. It leaves out facts that the inventory already states. It never includes routing settings.
2. **Project instruction files.** `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md`, each cut to `MAX_PROJECT_DOC_CHARS` (12000).
3. **Custom instructions.** `instructions.all`, then the entry of the agent in `instructions.agents`.

## Submit contract

Every agent ends with a call to `submit_<agent>` (the snake-case name). The input follows the schema from `submit_schema`. The `status` is `ok`, `stuck`, or `handoff`. These rules apply:

- A submit with an invalid shape returns an error to the agent, and the agent calls again.
- A submit with status `ok` fails if the declared report file does not exist. `code-reviewer` is the exception.
- A stuck submit needs a `diagnostic` and a `need`.
- Typed documents (`Document` tool) and book submits go through extra checks (`check_submit`).

See the page Change recipes for the steps that add an agent.

sections.title: Native executor and model providers
sections.summary: Describes the native agent loop, context compaction, the tool-call path, resume, and the provider layer with its retry policy.
sections.body:
Some users have API keys and no harness subscription. The native executor runs one agent on an API key. It owns the model loop and sends every tool call through the policy before the tool runs. `NativeExecutor` in `ostra-exec-native` implements `Executor`.

## The loop

`NativeExecutor::run` wraps `Run::execute` in a timeout. It stops on the cancel token or after `timeout_secs`. After a stop it gives the loop 3 seconds to clean up (`CLEANUP_GRACE`). A timeout gives the status `Error` and the text `timed out after N s`.

`execute` does these steps:

1. Split `route.model` into provider and model. A missing key returns the error that tells the user to set the key in the environment or the OS keychain.
2. Open the MCP tools for the workspace.
3. Build the policy (`ExecutionPolicy`) from the `ExecContext` and the build and test commands of the project.
4. Build `ToolEnv` and wrap `Bash` in the sandbox when the sandbox mode allows it.
5. Build the tool list: tools for the capabilities, the `Document` tool, MCP tools, and the `submit_<agent>` tool with its schema.
6. Send the first message, or rebuild the conversation from the stored transcript on a resume.
7. Loop until the agent submits, up to `MAX_TURNS` (400) model turns. After that the execution fails with an error that names the missing submit call.

## One tool call

1. `ToolEnv::canonical_call` makes paths absolute. The policy, the user, and the tool then see the same target.
2. `ExecutionPolicy::check` returns `Allow`, `Ask`, or `Deny`.
3. `Deny` returns the layer, the rule, and the reason to the model. `Ask` calls `ExecutionHost::ask_permission` and waits.
4. The tool runs. Read-only tools in one turn run at the same time: `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebFetch`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `Skill`, and the code tools.
5. The result goes back to the model. The executor shows at most `EMIT_LIMIT` (8 KiB) of an output in the Activity feed.
6. The policy observes the outcome. This feeds the build streak and the lesson gate.

## Context compaction

When the next request reaches `COMPACT_AT` (0.95) of the context window, the loop asks the model for a summary. The summary replaces all earlier messages. The window comes from the pricing table. It defaults to `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` (200,000 tokens). After a failed compaction, the loop waits until the context grows by `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` (2 percent of the window). Compaction needs a user turn last, so no tool call is open.

The output limit is the model maximum, or `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` (32,000 tokens). A cut-off response continues up to `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` (3) times.

## Resume

The host stores each message. A resume rebuilds the message list and gives each open tool call the result `Interrupted: this call did not finish.` The next user turn is the resume note, or `The previous run was interrupted. Continue from where it stopped.` A `compaction` record replaces all messages before it.

## Sandbox choice

`sandbox_for` calls `ostra_sandbox::decide`. If the mode needs a sandbox and none exists, the execution fails. In `auto` mode with no backend, `Bash` runs without a sandbox and the executor emits a status line. The server log warns once.

## Providers

`ostra-providers` gives one neutral chat interface. The types are `ChatRequest`, `Message`, `Block`, and `StreamEvent`. Two providers exist: Anthropic (Messages API) and OpenAI (Responses API). `ScriptedProvider` replays scripted answers for tests.

`Providers::for_model` takes `provider:model`. It returns `BadModel` for a malformed string. It returns `NoKey` when `anthropic` or `openai` has no key, and `UnknownProvider` for other names.

The retry policy has these values: `max_retries` 4, `base_delay` 1 second, `max_delay` 60 seconds, with jitter. A `Retry-After` header raises the delay. The policy never retries after output started.

A structured call (the judge path) forces a tool named `decide`. It makes at most 2 attempts, because some models reject a forced call. It sets `max_tokens` to 16,000.

## Credentials and prices

- The default provider variables are `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `OPENAI_BASE_URL`.
- A user can save keys in the console. They go into `registry.db`, sealed, and never into `config.toml`.
- Prices come from the models.dev catalog. The server caches it in the data dir and refreshes it once a day, so a restart without network still prices every execution. The `test-prices` feature of `ostra-core` gives fixed prices to tests.

sections.title: Harness executors and the hook bridge
sections.summary: Explains how Ostra runs an agent inside Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity, how it checks every tool call, and how it detects the end of an execution.
sections.body:
Some users prefer the CLI that they already pay for. A harness executor runs one agent inside that CLI under a PTY. Ostra cannot see the model loop, so it checks each tool call through hooks and reads the result through an MCP server. The crate is `ostra-exec-harness`.

## Harness kinds

| `HarnessKind` | CLI | Config table |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Claude` | Claude Code (`claude`) | `[harness.claude]` |
| `Codex` | Codex (`codex`) | `[harness.codex]` |
| `Grok` | Grok Build (`grok`) | `[harness.grok]` |
| `Agy` | Antigravity (`agy`) | `[harness.agy]` |

The `command` and `args` of each table come from the global `config.toml`. The route `harness:<name>` selects a harness for an agent.

## Start of an execution

`HarnessExecutor::launch` does these steps:

1. Check that the command exists. If not, the error starts with `harness-launch:`.
2. Write the per-execution config dir `<session>/.state/harness/<execution>`. It holds the hook config and the MCP registration.
3. Set the environment `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS`. The token is per execution.
4. Wrap the CLI in the sandbox, with the credential variables removed.
5. Start the CLI under a PTY and log the raw bytes to `terminal.log` (up to `TRANSCRIPT_CAP`).

The harness calls two subcommands of the same binary. `ostra hook` forwards each hook event. `ostra mcp-stdio` is an MCP server that registers under the name `ostra`.

## Checking a tool call

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as Harness CLI
    participant Hook as ostra hook
    participant Srv as ostra-server
    participant Bridge as HarnessBridge
    participant Pol as ExecutionPolicy
    CLI->>Hook: PreToolUse payload
    Hook->>Srv: POST /internal/policy
    Srv->>Bridge: handle request
    Bridge->>Pol: check ToolCall
    Pol-->>Bridge: Allow or Ask or Deny
    Bridge-->>Srv: PolicyResponse
    Srv-->>Hook: stdout and exit code
    Hook-->>CLI: decision in the harness format
```

Each harness has an adapter in `adapters/` that turns its hook payload into a canonical `ToolCall` (Claude Code names and input shapes). The adapter also formats the decision in the shape that the harness accepts. On `Ask`, the bridge calls `ExecutionHost::ask_permission`. The bridge refuses two kinds of call without the policy:

- A subagent spawn. Every Ostra agent is a leaf, so a delegated task runs outside the guards (`LEAF_REFUSAL`).
- A question to the user. Ostra asks through a gate, because nobody watches the terminal (`ASK_REFUSAL`).

Hook events are `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `Stop`, `SessionStart`, `PreInvocation`, and `PostInvocation`.

The MCP shim sends JSON-RPC to `POST /internal/mcp`. It serves the Ostra tools: `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, the code tools, the project tools, the coordination tools, and `submit_<agent>`. The shim speaks the MCP versions `2024-11-05`, `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. It leaves out `2026-07-28`, because Claude Code rejects its `tools/list` result.

## End of an execution

The submit call through the MCP shim completes the execution. Rules for the end:

- The harness `Stop` event confirms the end. If the CLI stops without a submit, the bridge turns it back.
- After the submit, the executor waits at most `AFTER_SUBMIT_GRACE` (20 seconds) for the turn to end.
- Antigravity has no `Stop` event. A submit followed by `AGY_QUIET_AFTER_SUBMIT` (4 seconds) of terminal quiet ends its turn.
- A session with no hook event and no output for `DEFAULT_IDLE_NUDGE` (240 seconds) gets a typed nudge, at most `MAX_IDLE_NUDGES` (2) times.

## Failures

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| The CLI is not installed. | Error `harness-launch: ...`. |
| The screen shows a sign-in text from `AUTH_MARKERS`, for example `not logged in`. | Error `harness-auth: ...`. |
| The CLI dies within `LAUNCH_WINDOW` (20 seconds). | A launch failure, not an execution failure. |
| The screen shows a fatal text from `FATAL_MARKERS`, for example `unknown model`. | The execution ends with `End::Fatal`. |

A `harness-` error opens a `HarnessFailure` gate. The user answers `retry` after login, or `native` to run on the native executor.

## Trust prompts and model offers

The executor answers a folder-trust prompt by harness:

- **Claude Code:** yes. Ostra loads only user settings and only its own MCP config, so trust adds nothing from the repository.
- **Codex:** `Open restricted` only. `Trust and continue` loads the `.codex/` config and hooks of the repository, so the executor refuses it.
- **Grok Build:** never. The user must trust the folder in Grok.

A new-model offer at startup keeps the routed model, because accepting the offer changes the user default.

## Other duties

- During an execution, the executor checks the repositories every `GIT_CHECK_EVERY` (2 seconds) for a planted `commondir`. It undoes the change and reports a `git-metadata` denial.
- The user can type into the terminal and resize it over the WebSocket. The server writes to the PTY.
- An ended execution keeps its terminal transcript. The console replays it read-only.
- `ExecutorKind::stream` tells the console to show an Activity feed for native executions and a terminal for harness executions.

sections.title: Policy engine: guards and permissions
sections.summary: Describes the two layers that check every tool call, the guard catalog, permission modes and rule syntax, and the build-streak and lesson gates.
sections.body:
A model can call a tool with a harmful target, and a shell command can hide the target. The policy engine checks every tool call from every executor before the call runs. `ExecutionPolicy::check` in `ostra-policy` returns `Allow`, `Ask`, or `Deny`.

## Two layers

1. **Layer 1: guards.** Nothing overrides a guard. A guard denial stands in every permission mode, and under YOLO.
2. **Layer 2: permissions.** The permission mode and the allow, ask, and deny rules decide.

Under YOLO, layer 2 turns each `Ask` into an `Allow` with the rule `yolo`. The mode `bypass` also reports as `yolo`. Denials stand.

A denial text starts with the correction and names the rule second. Some harnesses cut a reason to 256 characters, so the correction must come first.

## Guard catalog

| Guard | Refuses |
| --- | --- |
| `secret-read` | A read of the data dir, the master key file, or a credential store under the home folder. |
| `self-protection` | A write to the `ostra` binary, its config, or its databases. |
| `git-metadata` | A direct write under `.git`. Git commands are the only way. |
| `state-ownership` | A write to engine state: `.state`, the databases, the lesson store, or a review ledger that the agent does not own. |
| `artifact-ownership` | A write to `ostra-spec-*`, `ostra-plan-*`, or `ostra-research-*` files by an agent that does not own them. |
| `document-tool` | A direct write to a file that the `Document` tool renders. |
| `no-tests-from-implementer` | A test file written by `implementer`. |
| `write-scope` | A write outside the repo root and the session dir. Session-only agents can write only in their session dir. |
| `report-path` | A report at any path but the declared `Report file`. |
| `workspace-artifacts` | A write to workspace artifacts. Agents read them, and only the user changes them. |
| `workspace-docs` | A write under the books folder. |
| `manage-tools` | A `ProjectCreate` call from any agent but the implementer of a phase that creates a project, or a malformed call. |
| `lesson-gate` | A submit or report before the agent records a lesson for a recovery. |
| `build-streak` | A build or test command after 5 failures in a row. |

Two more refusals apply to consult executions: a write by an execution that only answers, and a submit by an execution that owes a reply.

The setting `tool_enforcement` (default `disabled`) controls the guards `write-scope`, `report-path`, `self-protection`, and the shell and interpreter checks behind them. When it is `disabled`, an agent can reach files by any route. The secret-read, git-metadata, state-ownership, artifact-ownership, and no-tests guards, the permission rules, and the sandbox still apply (Rule G1).

The ownership tables:

| File pattern | Owners |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra-review-ledger*.md` | `code-reviewer`, `implementer`, `write-test` |
| `ostra-security-block.json` | `code-reviewer` |
| `ostra-implementer-progress*.md` | `implementer` |
| `ostra-spec-*` | `generate-spec` |
| `ostra-plan-*` | `plan` |
| `ostra-research-*` | `explore` |

## Shell commands

`bash::parse` splits a command into simple commands with tree-sitter-bash. Guards check the targets that each command writes. A command with a write target that Ostra cannot resolve is not safe to allow silently. PowerShell and `cmd` are opaque, so the guards scan the raw text for protected paths, and the permission layer never allows them on its own.

## Permission modes

| `PermissionMode` | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `default` | Ask for edits and for commands that no rule allows. |
| `acceptEdits` | Allow edits inside the project and simple file commands (`mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, `mv`) in scope. |
| `plan` | Read-only. Deny everything that is not a read. |
| `bypass` | No asks. |

The workspace permission mode lives in the registry. A folder file never sets it.

### Rules

Rules use the syntax of Claude Code: `Tool` or `Tool(spec)`.

- `Bash(npm run test *)`: a glob over one simple command.
- `Edit(src/**)`, `Write(...)`, `Read(~/.ssh/**)`: gitignore-style paths. `//x` is absolute. `~/x` is under home. `x/y` is relative to the repo root. `Edit` rules cover every file-writing tool, and `Read` rules cover `Grep` and `Glob`.
- `WebFetch(domain:docs.rs)`: the host or any subdomain.

Deny beats ask, and ask beats allow. Rules merge in the order global, workspace, session. The global default has one deny rule: `Bash(rm -rf /*)`. `validate_rule` checks a rule when the user saves settings.

### What mode and rules decide

- Reads: allowed unless a rule asks or denies.
- Edits: always allowed in the session dir and in temp. In `acceptEdits`, allowed in the repo. Paths that run code later (hooks, for example) ask.
- Bash: the policy allows a read-only command that writes only in the session dir or temp. A command that Ostra cannot split, or a script with assignments, `export`, or loops, asks (`unparsed`, `unmodelled`). In `plan` mode it is denied.
- `WebFetch`: asks unless a rule allows it.
- MCP tools of workspace servers: allowed unless a rule says otherwise. In `plan` mode only tools that the server marks read-only are allowed.
- `ProjectCreate`: asks in every mode, whatever the allow rules say. YOLO answers it. A deny rule still refuses it (Rule O1).

The answer `AlwaysInWorkspace` adds a suggested rule to `permissions.allow`.

## Build streak and lessons

The policy watches build and test outcomes for each execution. `build::is_build_command` matches the commands in `project.toml`. When none exist, it uses a fallback list of common build tools.

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RECALL_THRESHOLD` | 2 | After 1 failure, recall known lessons so a known fix arrives at attempt 2. |
| `WARN_THRESHOLD` | 3 | Warn the agent. |
| `DENY_THRESHOLD` | 5 | Deny further build and test commands. The agent must submit `status: stuck`. |

After the agent recovers from a streak, the `lesson-gate` guard blocks its report and its `ok` submit until it records a lesson with the `Memory` tool. If the fix teaches nothing reusable, the agent calls `Report` with a `reason`.

## Containment

Three guards also count as containment signals: `secret-read`, `self-protection`, and `git-metadata`. The third signal of one execution pauses the session. Other guards refuse ordinary mistakes and are not signals.
